newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU accounting rules boost Italy's EMU hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU accounting rules boost Italy's EMU hopes.

text.p: The European Union handed Italy a glimmer of hope on Monday in its quest to join the single currency in 1999 but stopped short of giving a blessing to Rome's controversial "euro tax."

It also said Belgium, the Netherlands and other countries could sell gold to help cut their national debt, but that sales could not be used to reduce public deficits to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).
In an attempt to harmonise accounting standards across the 15-nation bloc, Eurostat, the EU's statistical body, issued a series of rulings on how to keep the books
Its decisions regarding the treatment of interest on zero coupon bonds and postal bonds would trim 0.26 percent from Italy's projected deficit to gross domestic product ratio.

A jubilant Italian government said this meant the European Commission's forecast of its 1997 budget deficit would be cut to 3.0 percent from 3.3 percent, qualifying it for the single currency - due to be launched in 1999.

But the highly technical and somewhat esoteric Eurostat report, covering eight accounting issues, side-stepped for now the decision about whether proposals such as Italy's "euro tax" could be used to lower deficits to meet the euro test.
Italy has proposed a euro tax to help it qualify for the currency by raising 5.5 trillion lire ($3.4 billion).

Eurostat officials said a decision on the one-off levy would be made by the end of February along with rulings on other important issues, such as the accounting of financial guarantees for state railways.

The report also addressed the budgetary effects of interest and currency swaps, gold sales, fungible bonds, financial leasing and pension funds, and sought to clarify the budgetary classification of national bodies which act on behalf of the EU.

On gold sales, Eurostat explicitly confirmed what many had already known -- that sales of the precious metal can be applied towards reducing the level of outstanding public debt but not to annual budget deficits.
While reluctant to numerically tally the net effect of their decisions, officials cautiously put forward an assessment of their report for several countries.

For Germany, Monday's decisions had no impact. Upcoming announcements on the treatment of state guarantees on loans to public sector companies, however, would likely have a large influence on many countries, including Germany.
For Britain, Eurostat said that approximately 100 million pounds ($160 million) -- 0.13 percent of GDP -- would be affected by their ruling on financial leasing.
Specifically, if a government sells real estate and rents it back with the intention of acquiring it at the end of the lease, the receipts from the sale could be applied to its deficit.
However, officials were not able to assess whether in Britain's case a reduction in the deficit would be realisable.

For Finland, the judgment on pension funds would leave their budgetary situation unchanged. Eurostat decided that pension funds which finance benefits on a pay-as-you-go basis would have to be classified among social security funds.
The EU statistical body also said governments would be able to sell real estate holdings to lower their annual deficits, making a distinction with financial assets, such as gold.
The central banks the Netherlands has recently sold a large amount of gold in order to shore-up its public finances.

Regarding the privatisation of state-run companies, revenue from such decisions could be applied towards a reduction of debt outstanding but not annual deficits. ($ = 1617 Italian Lire) ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
